Dusk versus Omnipair v1: capital efficiency and toxic flow

Sep 7, 2026, 6:43 AM UTC

Executive Summary

  • Fixed 10× remains the profit benchmark in the expanded test. It earns 4,600 USDT per six-hour evaluation run on average, versus 1,819 for the selected profitability controller, 3,635 for the volume controller and 3,319 for the volatility controller. All include LP-owned base, volatility and outward fees, plus trading losses.
  • Changing concentration can create its own arbitrage loss. The profitability controller collects more fees but spends 2,676 USDT per run on immediate arbitrage after changing the curve. Reserves are preserved; the marginal price changes.
  • A cost gate makes adaptation much more credible, without establishing a profit advantage. The exploratory cost-gated controller earns 4,509 USDT, 2.0% below fixed 10×, and has 26.6% lower mean trading drawdown. It needs fresh-date validation before selecting it as a risk control.
  • Current Dusk cannot run this minute-scale policy through its existing concentration update. Governance has a seven-day delay and protected-depth funding constraints. Prices are historical, customer demand is modeled, and the fast controller is a research design.

Compare equal capital and equal execution quality separately

Capital here is initial ordinary reserve NAV marked at an independent external price. The analytical baseline starts centered, balanced, fully cash-backed, without borrowing or hLP. For live comparisons, also report cash, lender claims, external borrower collateral and total external equity separately; eliminate internal funding claims when consolidating the system.

Execution efficiency means usable trade size for a specified all-in execution cost per dollar of capital. LVR means the cost of stale-price rebalancing against a frictionless strategy with the same inventory exposure; it is different from impermanent loss versus holding. Toxic-flow loss means adverse selection attributable to informed trading, measured with signed external-price markouts and explicit fee accounting.

Run both equal-capital and equal-trade-size/slippage experiments. At equal centered depth, the local dollar LVR benchmark is also equal, although Dusk uses less capital. That does not make the return per dollar safer.

The objective is trading only: LP-owned fees plus signed execution edge, with between-trade inventory price gains removed. Both dynamic fee components remain enabled for Dusk. Immediate switch losses are already included; subtracting them or LVR again would double-count.

SELECT *, (sum_fees+sum_edge)/cases AS mean_net_trading, sum_fees/cases AS mean_fees, 1.0*sum_switches/cases AS mean_switches, sum_switch_loss/cases AS mean_switch_loss, sum_drawdown/cases AS mean_drawdown FROM totals;

Decisions use past data, with reserves carried through every change

Training uses January 8–9 and evaluation uses January 15 and 19, with new demand seeds. Each day supplies four separate continuous six-hour blocks at one-second resolution. Every block starts balanced, centered and cold; there is no reset inside the six hours. Twelve fixed/controller candidates train on two seeds, then one controller from each signal family and the best fixed benchmark are frozen before the main evaluation on three seeds. Some hours were inspected in the preceding analysis, so this is not a fully blind validation set.

All adaptive policies start at 5×, observe a ten-minute warmup, decide once per minute and wait at least five minutes between changes. They can move one step among 3×, 5× and 10×. Decisions happen before the next reference tick and arriving orders. Fixed pools run throughout the same warmup; all six hours count toward profit.

The profitability signal uses completed 30-second markouts for all swaps over the preceding five-minute maturity window. It divides fees plus favorable execution markouts by adverse markout losses, with a 1-USDT denominator floor. The selected thresholds are 1.05 and 1.5: choose 3× below the lower threshold, 10× above the upper one and 5× in between. The controller sees no customer/arbitrage labels or rejected intentions. Volume and volatility controls use only past executed turnover and external returns.

Demand is modeled as either steady strong, steady weak, steady cheap execution, or randomly changing half-hour regimes. Prior January 1 CEX clips supply only a size proxy; directions, arrivals and cost tolerance remain explicit assumptions. Every paired policy receives identical offered orders and budgets, with fills responding to its own quotes.

Extra fee income did not cover the losses created by reconfiguration

The profitability controller earns 8,131Source for 8,131Source: Adaptive concentration: historical prices with modeled demandTables: totals (from adaptive_replays.csv and adaptive_gated_replays.csv), adaptive_replay.py, adaptive_plan.json, adaptive_selection.json, adaptive_diagnostics.py, market-data/manifest.json USDT in LP fees, versus 6,305Source for 6,305Source: Adaptive concentration: historical prices with modeled demandTables: totals (from adaptive_replays.csv and adaptive_gated_replays.csv), adaptive_replay.py, adaptive_plan.json, adaptive_selection.json, adaptive_diagnostics.py, market-data/manifest.json at fixed 10Source for 10Source: Adaptive concentration: historical prices with modeled demandTables: totals (from adaptive_replays.csv and adaptive_gated_replays.csv), adaptive_replay.py, adaptive_plan.json, adaptive_selection.json, adaptive_diagnostics.py, market-data/manifest.json×, yet finishes much worse. It changes concentration 30.2 times per six-hour run on average. Immediate arbitrage following those changes costs 2,676Source for 2,676Source: Adaptive concentration: historical prices with modeled demandTables: totals (from adaptive_replays.csv and adaptive_gated_replays.csv), adaptive_replay.py, adaptive_plan.json, adaptive_selection.json, adaptive_diagnostics.py, market-data/manifest.json USDT, compared with a 2,781Source for 2,781Source: Adaptive concentration: historical prices with modeled demandTables: totals (from adaptive_replays.csv and adaptive_gated_replays.csv), adaptive_replay.py, adaptive_plan.json, adaptive_selection.json, adaptive_diagnostics.py, market-data/manifest.json-USDT total profit gap. The switch-loss comparison identifies an accounting component; it is not a claim that simply adding it back reproduces a no-switch counterfactual.

Changing the curve leaves both token balances intact, but it changes their implied marginal price. Arbitrageurs can trade against that new price. The volatility accumulator is preserved, all fees apply, and greedy profitable arbitrage is settled before the next external-price tick. There is no free recenter, capital injection or inventory reset.

The profitability controller trails fixed 10Source for 10Source: Adaptive concentration: historical prices with modeled demandTables: totals (from adaptive_replays.csv and adaptive_gated_replays.csv), adaptive_replay.py, adaptive_plan.json, adaptive_selection.json, adaptive_diagnostics.py, market-data/manifest.json× on both evaluation days. The January 19 day is worse, but the result is not confined to that day. Delayed profitability can also respond to trades induced by the controller itself; a fee-rich signal does not establish profitable incremental demand.

SELECT *, (sum_fees+sum_edge)/cases AS mean_net_trading, sum_fees/cases AS mean_fees, 1.0*sum_switches/cases AS mean_switches, sum_switch_loss/cases AS mean_switch_loss, sum_drawdown/cases AS mean_drawdown FROM totals;

The current concentration update cannot execute these fast changes

The existing path is a governance parameter update with a seven-day timelock after support approval. A minute-scale controller would need an explicit design for delegated or automatic authority; this analysis changes no protocol code.

Reconfiguration also requires a protected-depth budget. A depth decrease must be covered at 125%Source for 125%Source: Current Dusk concentration update and protected-depth rulesFile: adaptive_extra_validation.json, plus a 1Source for 1Source: Current Dusk concentration update and protected-depth rulesFile: adaptive_extra_validation.json-bp guard on current depth, and fit a hard cap of 1%Source for 1%Source: Current Dusk concentration update and protected-depth rulesFile: adaptive_extra_validation.json of depth. At centered unchanged reserves, moving from 10Source for 10Source: Current Dusk concentration update and protected-depth rulesFile: adaptive_extra_validation.json× to 5Source for 5Source: Current Dusk concentration update and protected-depth rulesFile: adaptive_extra_validation.json× requires 62.51%Source for 62.51%Source: Current Dusk concentration update and protected-depth rulesFile: adaptive_extra_validation.json of current depth under this formula; moving from 10Source for 10Source: Current Dusk concentration update and protected-depth rulesFile: adaptive_extra_validation.json× to 3Source for 3Source: Current Dusk concentration update and protected-depth rulesFile: adaptive_extra_validation.json× requires 87.51%Source for 87.51%Source: Current Dusk concentration update and protected-depth rulesFile: adaptive_extra_validation.json. Both exceed that hard cap. Distributing fees to LPs does not automatically create the in-pool protected-depth budget.

The economic replays deliberately relax these admission rules so the switching hypothesis can be tested. Reserve conservation and repricing loss are modeled, but those results are not executable current-program returns. Changing how depth protection treats a different curve shape is a separate design question; bypassing the guard is not established as safe.

Source for The current concentration update cannot execute these fast changesSource: Current Dusk concentration update and protected-depth rulesFile: adaptive_extra_validation.json

The arithmetic is feasible off chain; protocol integration remains unmeasured

The local research engine completed 1,440 primary replays in about 134 seconds. A small warm Python benchmark rebuilt a reserve-preserving curve in roughly 0.066 ms per call. These are local CPU observations, not Solana compute-unit measurements or a production latency guarantee.

The policy needs an external price reference and delayed swap markouts. Its work scales with observed swaps; the queues store pending 30-second markouts and recent five-minute observations. Pool fee revenue or its internal volatility accumulator alone does not identify toxic flow. An implementation must address reference quality, manipulation and the cost of keeping these observations.

Current Rust curve reconstruction already uses a bounded branch selection and quadratic-root approach. The new economic risk lies in deciding when a change is worth its repricing loss, along with authorization and protected-depth accounting. No automatic controller, integer parity or compute-unit test was implemented here.

Keep fixed 10× as the profit benchmark and test cost-aware adaptation for risk

The evidence supports a fixed benchmark and a narrowly defined next experiment. Fixed 10× leads this test grid on mean trading profit. Fixed 3× remains relevant for weak demand, and cheap execution can favor v1. A lower concentration should be selected with the demand regime and execution objective in view.

For adaptive concentration, take only the cost-gated candidate forward to fresh dates, with a risk objective declared before testing—for example, acceptable trading drawdown at a specified profit concession. Compare it with fixed 3×, 5× and 10× again. Require causal signals, an estimate of repricing cost, and enough evidence that the incremental benefit can pay that cost.

The current sample cannot establish real-world demand capture, market-frequency weights, robustness to strategic manipulation, or a production policy. It has four historical days, two later-date evaluation days and modeled customer demand. Protected-depth semantics and controller authority remain separate unresolved design requirements.

Historical prices replace the invented paths; demand is explicit

The comparison now uses five historical SOL/USDT hours. Use observed clip sizes without calling them Dusk customer demand

The size proxy comes from 238,579 aggregated trade clips on January 1, before every test episode. Median notional is 208.97 USDT; the 90th percentile is 3104.32, and the 99th is 18190.22. The full empirical distribution is sampled without trimming. An aggregate CEX clip is not necessarily a complete customer order and does not identify non-toxic flow.

Customer intentions arrive through a Poisson process calibrated to expected offered volume of 100,000 or 1 million USDT per hour. Sizes are bootstrapped from that earlier distribution; directions are independently 50/50. Each customer draws an individual lognormal cost budget, with median 20, 50, 100 or 200 bps and log-standard-deviation 0.5. A trade fills only if its all-in quote meets that customer's budget. Actual offered and filled volumes vary by seed, and every concentration receives the same intentions and budgets within a paired case.

These are explicit assumptions about Dusk demand. The observed CEX volume does not establish pool capture, customer fee tolerance, clustered arrivals or directional predictability. The test contains 820 primary replays, 120 arbitrage-interval checks and 75 replays with less starting capital: 1,015 total.

Trading P&L includes every executed customer and arbitrage trade: LP fees plus signed execution edge at the contemporaneous external reference. Price-change gains and losses on inventory between trades are removed using an independent ledger. Do not interpret these values as total unhedged LP returns, and do not subtract LVR again.

It reports mean net trading bps relative to each pool's own initial capital. Every concentration is replayed on its actual resized curve; no P&L is merely scaled from the equal-capital result. 10Source for 10Source: Historical-price replay with modeled customer demandTables: source_rows (totals from shortlist_replays.csv), shortlist_replays.csv, shortlist_replay.py, fee_optimizer.py× has the highest mean trading P&L per capital in all five of these matched-capital cases.

This does not establish equal risk or execution throughout the hour. Later prices, fee signals and quotes diverge, and the smaller pools receive more offered volume relative to their capital. The comparison is conditional on being offered the same absolute intentions.

The main tradeoff survives the tested timing change

Arbitrage timing is checked using identical seeds. The latency extension compares opportunities every 1, 5 and 30 seconds while continuing to observe the same 1-second reference prices and processing customer intentions at their scheduled boundaries. The comparison uses the first three seeds, 1 million expected offered volume and 100-bps median budgets for every interval.

For those matched seeds, 5× leads in the quiet hour at all three intervals; 10× leads in the other four hours at all three intervals. This also illustrates why comparing five seeds at 1 second with only three at a slower interval would be misleading. The stored per-seed rows allow exactly paired comparisons.

The numerical optimizer now checks both the uncapped and capped outward-fee regimes. A coarse grid missed a second profit peak in an extreme-volatility replay. The revised solver agrees with an independent1,600-point search on four full extreme-hour replays and 60 randomized off-center opportunities. This is research-model computation; no on-chain compute-unit measurement is claimed.

Advance 10× for strong demand, retain 3× and 5× as conditional alternatives

The evidence favors a conditional shortlist. 10× is the leading candidate when offered volume is substantial and customers accept the fee schedule. 3× provides the lower-exposure alternative when demand or fee tolerance is weak. 5× remains an intermediate candidate, including the quiet-hour runs where its advantage over 10× depends on the order sample.

Before choosing a live parameter or automatic controller, the controlling unknown is the target market's actual demand response: order sizes, available alternative quotes, willingness to pay, directional clustering and arrival intensity. Historical CEX prices and clip sizes do not measure those quantities for Dusk.

An adaptive controller should subsequently be evaluated against these fixed baselines on the same opportunities, including any price movement or value transfer caused by changing amplification. This run does not implement that controller or change protocol parameters.

Data and accounting checks passed, with a defined scope

The archives are checksum verified and the selected price paths reconcile. The source check covers44,640 minute rows, 345, 600 second rows and238,579 prior-day aggregate clips. It checks timestamp units, continuous unique bar keys, OHLC bounds, finite prices, volumes and clip identifiers. All 300 selected minute closes and quote volumes reconcile with the corresponding second rows.

Every replay reconciles fee components, customer and arbitrage trading P&L, offered/fill counts, and an independent endpoint inventory ledger. Displayed means are recomputed in SQLite from sums and seed counts. The full raw seed rows, source hashes, source URLs, cost-budget assumptions and executed notebook cells accompany the report.

Limits: one CEX price proxy, five selected independent hours, five demand seeds, and unobserved Dusk customer demand. No regime-frequency weighting, annualized return, continuous-month performance, subsecond execution, strategic transaction splitting, integer program parity, recentering, adaptive amplification, fee compounding, hLP or borrowing is claimed. All monetary values are USDT quote units; no USD peg conversion is performed.

Fix fee parameters and vary concentration

Only amplification changes across Dusk configurations: 1.25×, 1.5×, 2×, 3×, 4×, 5×, 7.5×, 10×, 15×, 20×, 30× and 50×. Every configuration keeps the 100-bps core, 400-bps additional shoulder and a positive full-range tail. Fixed fees: 30-bps base, outward coefficient 10, volatility coefficient 1, 200-bps cap per surcharge, and 60-second volatility half-life. Fixing parameters does not fix realized fees: each fee still responds to its trade and prior observed pool-price movements.

Equal-capital tests start with $1m ordinary reserves. Equal-execution tests resize each independent pool to match v1's order output, then recompute shock losses on that actual capital. All surcharges are distributed to LPs; the protocol takes 20% of the base fee. Widths, center and concentration remain fixed throughout each path.

Trading-only P&L = LP fees plus signed execution edge against the external price at each trade. Both customer and arbitrage trades count. Inventory gains caused by external-price moves between trades are removed and reconciled using an independent endpoint inventory ledger. These are event losses and synthetic one-hour results, without an APR interpretation.

SELECT *, pre_fee_edge+lp_fees AS net_trading_usd, -(pre_fee_edge+lp_fees) AS net_loss_usd,
10000*(pre_fee_edge+lp_fees)/capital AS net_trading_bps,
10000*(notional/output-1) AS cost_bps, 1-matched_capital/capital AS capital_saved
FROM modeled ORDER BY kind,amplification,state,path,notional,jump;

Trading profits depend on the path and on which orders fill

The paths include all trading profits and losses. Each run lasts one synthetic hour, starts cold and centered with $1mSource for $1mSource: Fixed-fee concentration experiments and metric cross-checkTables: modeled (inline synthetic outputs), concentration_results.json, concentration_sweep.py, samples external prices every 30Source for 30Source: Fixed-fee concentration experiments and metric cross-checkTables: modeled (inline synthetic outputs), concentration_results.json, concentration_sweep.py seconds, and offers the same 60Source for 60Source: Fixed-fee concentration experiments and metric cross-checkTables: modeled (inline synthetic outputs), concentration_results.json, concentration_sweep.py seeded buy/sell intentions. An order fills only when all-in cost is at most 150 bps versus the current external price. Arbitrage runs before and after accepted orders; both fees follow the pool's own evolving state.

The table uses $2kSource for $2kSource: Fixed-fee concentration experiments and metric cross-checkTables: modeled (inline synthetic outputs), concentration_results.json, concentration_sweep.py per intended order ($120kSource for $120kSource: Fixed-fee concentration experiments and metric cross-checkTables: modeled (inline synthetic outputs), concentration_results.json, concentration_sweep.py offered per hour). At a flat external price, v1 earns $472.88Source for $472.88Source: Fixed-fee concentration experiments and metric cross-checkTables: modeled (inline synthetic outputs), concentration_results.json, concentration_sweep.py and Dusk 5Source for 5Source: Fixed-fee concentration experiments and metric cross-checkTables: modeled (inline synthetic outputs), concentration_results.json, concentration_sweep.py× earns $588.20Source for $588.20Source: Fixed-fee concentration experiments and metric cross-checkTables: modeled (inline synthetic outputs), concentration_results.json, concentration_sweep.py. With a quiet-to-5%Source for -5%Source: Fixed-fee concentration experiments and metric cross-checkTables: modeled (inline synthetic outputs), concentration_results.json, concentration_sweep.py jump, v1 earns $226.57Source for $226.57Source: Fixed-fee concentration experiments and metric cross-checkTables: modeled (inline synthetic outputs), concentration_results.json, concentration_sweep.py while Dusk 5Source for 5Source: Fixed-fee concentration experiments and metric cross-checkTables: modeled (inline synthetic outputs), concentration_results.json, concentration_sweep.py× loses $137.66Source for $137.66Source: Fixed-fee concentration experiments and metric cross-checkTables: modeled (inline synthetic outputs), concentration_results.json, concentration_sweep.py. Both surcharges are active, but concentration does not win on every path.

The slow trend compounds evenly to +5%Source for +5%Source: Fixed-fee concentration experiments and metric cross-checkTables: modeled (inline synthetic outputs), concentration_results.json, concentration_sweep.py; the jump reaches +5%Source for +5%Source: Fixed-fee concentration experiments and metric cross-checkTables: modeled (inline synthetic outputs), concentration_results.json, concentration_sweep.py halfway through and stays there. The choppy path completes ten smooth cycles around the center with roughly ±1%Source for 1%Source: Fixed-fee concentration experiments and metric cross-checkTables: modeled (inline synthetic outputs), concentration_results.json, concentration_sweep.py price movement. Fills are allowed to differ between pools; these are common opportunities, not identical forced executions. Runs without customer orders isolate adverse selection.

Source for Trading profits depend on the path and on which orders fillSource: Fixed-fee concentration experiments and metric cross-checkTables: modeled (inline synthetic outputs), concentration_results.json, concentration_sweep.py

Actual independent metric recomputation from synthetic source-derived curve/fee outputs. Methods: concentration_sweep.py. Complete raw data: concentration_results.json. Code fingerprints: concentration_validation.json. This is not observed market data.

SELECT *, pre_fee_edge+lp_fees AS net_trading_usd, -(pre_fee_edge+lp_fees) AS net_loss_usd,
10000*(pre_fee_edge+lp_fees)/capital AS net_trading_bps,
10000*(notional/output-1) AS cost_bps, 1-matched_capital/capital AS capital_saved
FROM modeled ORDER BY kind,amplification,state,path,notional,jump;

Routing assumptions change the winner

Exact optima are fragile under this demand model. A sensitivity grid tests v1 and Dusk at 2×, 3×, 4×, 5×, 10×, 20× and 50×. It uses routing limits of 100 and 300 bps with the original order sequence, plus two additional order-direction seeds at 150 bps: 256 additional runs, with all fee parameters unchanged.

For $10k orders on the choppy path, 50× leads the original 150-bps run and both alternate sequences. Tightening the limit to 100 bps makes 4× lead the sensitivity grid; loosening it to 300 bps makes 10× lead. Flat-price, smaller-order rankings also vary. Hard routing thresholds produce discontinuous fills, so these are scenario winners, not smoothly fitted optimal parameters.

Retain 3×, 5× and 10× for the next calibrated comparison: a lower-exposure candidate, an intermediate candidate with substantial execution gains, and a candidate testing whether extra captured demand pays for larger jump losses. Keep 20–50× as stress cases. This is an experimental shortlist, not a deployment recommendation.

Concentration cannot remove the minimum fee toll

A warm $1k order cannot match v1 at any tested concentration, or even at infinite depth in this model. At an accumulator of 0.005, base plus volatility takes approximately 79.60 bps of gross input. Expressed as all-in cost per unit received, that is 80.24 bps before outward surcharge or price impact. V1's $1k quote costs 50.09 bps including impact. The cool and hot states also fail this target.

These cases are recorded as unattainable_fee_floor, with null capital rather than a fabricated large-capital solution. The fees stay unchanged as requested. A later small-order optimization would need to revisit fee settings or the execution target.

Calibrate demand before testing an automatic concentration rule

This sweep supports conditional concentration choices, not a rule that higher volatility should automatically increase concentration. Next compare the shortlisted fixed configurations using realistic order intentions and external-price updates, then test an explicit controller against those fixed baselines. Changing amplification can move the quoted price and transfer value; that economic cost belongs in the controller comparison.

The model uses real-valued input-denominated fees; no integer program parity or compute-unit claim is made. Both pools distribute fees without compounding. No hLP, debt, retained fees or center movement is included. Greedy arbitrage observes these synthetic prices every 30 seconds, which is not a Solana block-time model. Price movements within those intervals are unobserved. Fees paid in base are valued as if immediately converted at the external mark.

The scenarios have no estimated occurrence probabilities. Three order sequences and three cost limits are sensitivity tests, not confidence intervals. Trading-only P&L excludes directional inventory gains and does not subtract LVR again. The main unresolved quantity is actual profitable customer flow attracted by each concentration relative to adverse selection.

Gross LVR rises with the depth available to arbitrageurs

For a constant-product pool, gross local LVR divided by NAV is annual variance divided by eight per year. For Dusk’s active segment, differentiating its inventory curve gives local gross LVR = active liquidity × √price × variance / 4. At the centered point this becomes amplification × capital × variance / 8.

The chart expresses this local rate per day at 100% annual volatility. At 50% volatility every value is one quarter as large; at 150% it is 2.25× as large. Fees, discrete block timing, jumps and center changes require additional modeling. Do not read these bars as realized fee-paying arbitrage losses.

Dynamic fees must compensate for the extra exposure

Let r be residual net adverse-selection cost divided by each configuration’s gross local LVR benchmark, after crediting fees from the same toxic trades to the selected LP owner. In the matched centered comparison, Dusk/v1 residual cost per dollar is approximately A × r_Dusk/r_v1.

At 5×, r_Dusk must be below one fifth of r_v1 to reduce net toxic cost per dollar. That is more than an 80% reduction in the residual factor relative to v1. At 2× the hurdle is more than 50%; at 10× it is more than 90%. These are break-even conditions, not estimates of achieved protection. Organic fee revenue can still make Dusk more profitable even when toxic cost is higher.

For a simple budget check, a 30-bps fee with 80% allocated to LPs yields 24 bps per dollar traded. Covering the unsuppressed local LVR benchmark requires daily turnover of 0.143× capital for v1 and 0.713× for the 5× case. Use this as a fee-income hurdle, not a forecast of required actual volume. In a residual-cost model, add organic fees only: toxic fees have already been credited in r.

Current code makes the fee and ownership assumptions decisive

Concentration and dynamic fees are configurable. The default AMM configuration is 1Source for 1Source: Dusk current local curve, fee and accounting implementationTables: programs/dusk/CONCENTRATION.md, programs/dusk/src/transitions/amm/curve.rs, programs/dusk/src/transitions/amm/fees.rs, programs/dusk/src/transitions/amm/mod.rs, programs/dusk/src/state/market.rs, programs/dusk/README.md× CPMM with zero widths and zero dynamic-fee coefficients; the protocol name alone implies no concentration gain.

The volatility charge uses the decayed accumulator from preceding successful swaps. That accumulator sums capped absolute relative price movements, not statistical variance. A first shock after quiet conditions therefore cannot rely on its own volatility update for protection. The distance charge can apply to the current outward path, but distance from an internal center is not a direct observation of informed flow; a stale center can misclassify economically useful repricing.

While recenter retention is armed, dynamic surcharge goes into protected, non-quoteable reserves outside ordinary yLP NAV and withdrawal claims. Do not count it simultaneously as immediately distributable LP income and as free center-adjustment capital. hLP funding is also an internal transfer when evaluating consolidated participants; synthetic hLP leverage is not extra trader-visible depth. An active-hLP replay must separately measure yLP, each hLP and protocol outcomes, plus settlement rejections.

The experiments check the formulas, accounting and repeated greedy execution. They do not optimize a strategic multi-transaction attack or reproduce the integer program, center admission, cash constraints or hLP settlement. To estimate daily net LVR, feed real price paths and trade demand through those mechanisms and track volatility updates, fee decay and recenter funding over time.

Synthetic conditional states using current Dusk input-denominated gross-path fees. Original computation: dynamic_fees.py; complete rows: dynamic_results.json. Source locations: AMM mod.rs 913-1033 and 1440-1535; fees.rs 395-484 and 594-626; ledger.rs 310-370.

-- Actual independent metric calculation from dynamic_fees.py curve/fee outputs.
-- $1m capital and +1% external jump for LP shortfalls; gross $10k buy for execution.
-- Source curve, fee ordering, optimizer and parameter/state assumptions remain
-- in dynamic_fees.py and dynamic_results.json; inputs below are synthetic.
WITH modeled(ordering, profile, curve_shortfall, base_fee, distance_fee,
             volatility_fee, ten_k_buy_output, matched_execution_capital) AS (
 VALUES
 (0, 'v1 base only', 11.303873771323879, 5.234123330376046, 0, 0.0, 9775.084808910382, 999999.9999996051),
 (1, '5x base only', 56.519322155938426, 26.170569951083674, 0, 0.0, 9930.397574473289, 261446.45083762181),
 (2, '5x dynamic, quiet', 37.21895248898363, 13.738331405265173, 5.030077537989562, 0.0, 9878.985929334944, 624195.2703272153),
 (3, '5x dynamic, warm', 16.70789645530067, 5.449901882870926, 0.31104682351776014, 9.01086596554281, 9830.532851481403, 737990.6255974406),
 (4, '5x dynamic, hot', 0.0, 0.0, 0, 0.0, 9782.550307696802, 949255.6985351259)
)
SELECT ordering, profile,
       curve_shortfall - (0.8*base_fee + distance_fee + volatility_fee) AS lp_loss_distributed_usd,
       curve_shortfall - 0.8*base_fee AS lp_loss_retained_usd,
       distance_fee + volatility_fee AS protected_bucket_if_retained_usd,
       10000*(10000/ten_k_buy_output-1) AS average_cost_bps,
       matched_execution_capital,
       1-matched_execution_capital/1000000 AS capital_saved_same_execution
FROM modeled ORDER BY ordering;

Parameterize five groups before choosing a configuration

  1. Curve: test A = 1, 2, 5 and 10; core/fade widths of 100/400 and 500/1,500 bps. Enforce a positive full-range tail. Width and amplification are coupled: 10× with 1,000/4,000-bps widths is infeasible in this model, with a strict upper bound near 8.69×.
  2. Fee response and ownership: vary base fee, distance coefficient/cap, volatility coefficient/cap/half-life, fee denomination, protocol allocation and recenter retention. Model organic demand response to all-in cost; do not assume higher fees leave volume unchanged.
  3. Center policy: vary EMA half-life, movement threshold, step and minimum interval. Compare funded moves and deferred moves; measure the economic cost and time spent away from useful depth.
  4. External flow: use annual volatility scenarios of 50%, 100%, 150% and 200%, plus jumps, trends, reversals, quiet-to-shock transitions, trade-size distributions and arbitrage latency. Retain the external reference-price path for markouts.
  5. Balance sheet: vary cash utilization, borrow interest and bad debt, hLP participation/funding, liquidity withdrawals and execution rejection rates. External yield can improve LP economics but is not evidence of reduced LVR.

Next: replay identical market opportunities through both engines

Start with 2× and 5× as candidates, not an optimum. Compare v1, Dusk at 1×, concentrated Dusk without dynamic fees, and concentrated Dusk with dynamic fees. Add recentering and active hLP as separate ablations so any advantage has an identifiable cause.

Use the same independent external-price path and the same exogenous organic trade intentions. Let arbitrage size, successful fills and organic routing respond to each pool’s actual quotes. Replaying identical executed fills would conceal the fee-demand tradeoff.

Record signed base quantity q (positive when the trader buys base), pre-fee execution price P_exec and independent midprice P_h after 1 second, 10 seconds and 60 seconds. Trader markout is q×(P_h−P_exec); LP execution edge is its negative plus LP-owned fees. Keep each horizon separate. Do not subtract both this markout and LVR from the same P&L, or credit a fee twice.

Judge configurations on net LP edge per time-weighted NAV, organic volume captured, all-in execution cost at matched size, cash fill capacity, rejected demand and drawdown. Report cohort results for ordinary yLP, each hLP side and the consolidated system.

The remaining evidence is market-specific

The next calibration needs a market or pair, a v1 reference configuration/state, and timestamped independent prices plus trade-intention or trade data. Which widths and fees win depends on whether flow is mean-reverting, trending, informed or price-sensitive. No historical dataset was supplied or used here; the generic volatile-token/stablecoin setup is an explicit assumption.

Scope and assumptions

This is a verified mathematical first pass against the inspected local source, with reproducible synthetic scenarios. Dusk is pre-deployment. The v1 checkout was not matched to a deployed binary, and current Dusk documentation contains pre-existing local edits.

The original benchmark uses floating-point nested constant-product inventory and fixed fees. The extension applies the current input-denominated dynamic-fee formulas to conditional one-shock and same-slot greedy-burst experiments. It does not reproduce atom rounding, integer-exact fee execution, block scheduling, cash constraints, hLP settlement, center admission, launch protections, lending or liquidations. Gross local LVR and the single-jump experiment answer different questions and must not be added together. A full replay remains necessary for measured net efficiency and an optimum parameter set.

  6. Independent metric calculation from modeled curve outputsverification_query.sql · SQLite · 2026-09-07T02:51:18.853581+00:00

    Actual executed cross-check of report metrics. Input outputs are computed by model.py, not observed trades. Original curve method and all scenarios are preserved in model.py and results.json.

    SQL query
    -- Inputs: inspected Dusk curve modeled in model.py, $1m initial capital,
-- $10k gross buy, 30-bps fixed input fee, 100% annual volatility.
-- Tail/shoulder ratios and base_out are floating-point curve outputs.
WITH curve_outputs(amplification, capital_usd, gross_quote, base_out,
                   fee_bps, tail_depth_vs_v1, shoulder_depth_vs_v1) AS (
  VALUES
    (1, 1000000, 10000, 9775.084808910266, 30, 1.0, 1),
    (2, 1000000, 10000, 9863.362567108183, 30, 0.9852543572112978, 1.4926271786056489),
    (5, 1000000, 10000, 9930.397574473289, 30, 0.9410174288451914, 2.970508714422596),
    (10, 1000000, 10000, 9950.159382192127, 30, 0.8672892149016801, 5.43364460745084)
)
SELECT *,
  CASE WHEN amplification=1 THEN 'v1 / 1×' ELSE 'Dusk ' || amplification || '×' END AS configuration,
  10000.0 * (gross_quote / base_out - 1) AS average_cost_bps,
  amplification * capital_usd * 1.0 / (8.0 * 365) AS gross_lvr_usd_day,
  1.0 - 1.0/amplification AS same_peak_depth_capital_saved
FROM curve_outputs
ORDER BY amplification;
